name: Gatun Locks
label: Gatun Locks
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gatún Locks View Deck' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Gatún locks view deck' (way/1511612760): middle (48 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM R12228857 (Gatun Locks): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Original 1914 Panama Canal locks where ships are lifted to Gatun Lake.

text.description: Gatun Locks is a working set of canal locks where ships are raised and lowered in three chambers, with Gatún Lake stretching away beyond. What makes it good for photos is that the action is close and easy to read: a large ship sits in a long stone-edged chamber, and you can watch it move up or down. The best-known place to watch from is the Gatún Locks View Deck, a raised platform beside the locks, reached from the Agua Clara Visitor Center. From up there you look along the chambers and out to the lake, so a single frame can include the ship, the lock walls and the water behind. A second option is the Gatún Locks Visitors Pavilion, which gives an elevated view down onto the locks and the ships passing through. Which of the two is open can change, so check on arrival. For phone photos, start wide to show the whole scene, then move in on the ship once something is happening. Ships move slowly, so you have time to try a wide shot, a closer one and a short Live Photo of the water level changing. Ask at the visitor centre when ships are expected, as a quiet chamber makes a much less interesting picture. Entry to the View Deck is part of the Agua Clara ticket, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Gatun Locks are on the Panama Canal in the Colón area, with Gatún Lake lying behind them. The View Deck is beside the locks, reached from the Agua Clara Visitor Center.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stops are listed for this spot, so travel from Colón to the Agua Clara Visitor Center. From the visitor centre, follow the way through to the Gatún Locks View Deck beside the locks. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the chambers and the lake in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a ship in the chamber, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the ship's bow or the lock gates.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Gatún Locks View Deck (beside the locks, reached from the Agua Clara Visitor Center). Ships rising and falling through the three Gatún chambers from a raised platform, with Gatún Lake visible beyond. If the deck is busy, the Gatún Locks Visitors Pavilion is an alternative with an elevated view down onto the locks.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the lock walls as leading lines, keeping them level with the grid. Place the ship in the lower third and leave the lake and sky above it. Take one wide shot with the whole chamber, then a closer one of the ship once it settles in the lock. A Live Photo can catch the movement of the water and the ship.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the ship to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Wipe the lens before you start, as a smudge shows up in bright light.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when a ship is due, as the scene is much better with one in the chamber. Ask the visitor centre for the transit schedule on the day.

text.access_note: The View Deck is reached through the Agua Clara Visitor Center and is included in its ticket, so check the official site before you go for current entry details and opening times.

name: Atlantic Bridge, Panama
label: Atlantic Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Puente Atlántico' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/974365873: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Atlantic Bridge' (3159 m across).
notes: Cable-stayed bridge over the canal's Atlantic entrance, photographed from ships.

text.description:
The Atlantic Bridge (Puente Atlántico) carries a road across the Atlantic entrance to the Panama Canal, near Colón. It opened in 2019 and is the third bridge over the canal, after the Bridge of the Americas and the Centennial Bridge on the Pacific side. It is a cable-stayed bridge with two towers. The main span is 530 metres, with a 230-metre span on each side, and it was built by Vinci Construction.

It photographs well because the shapes are clean and repeated: two tall towers, fans of cables and a long, smooth deck. Visitor reviews also say the view of the canal locks from the top is good on both sides, so you can pair the structure with the working waterway below. Take a few frames looking back along the deck towards the Agua Clara side, then turn round for the Fort San Lorenzo side.

The bridge carries heavy road traffic and there is little room to stop. Do not stand on the carriageway. Only stop where it is legal and safe, and keep your phone away from the traffic side. For a calmer view of the whole bridge, the Agua Clara visitor centre shows the lock chambers in the foreground with the bridge in the distance. Check the official site before you go, as that is a separate site that may have its own entry rules.

Keep the lens clean, as humid air often leaves a film on it, and take a few frames of each view so you can pick the sharpest.
text.geographic_location: The Atlantic Bridge is in the Colón area of Panama, where the Panama Canal meets the Atlantic. It is part of a local connection road that links Bolivar Highway in the east with the undeveloped area to the west. Agua Clara and Fort San Lorenzo are the two reference points for the views from the bridge.
text.directions_text: No station, tram stop or other public transport is listed for this spot, so check local options before you travel. The phone icon on the map is the middle of the bridge outline. You can only shoot there where it is legal and safe to stop, and no pull-off at that exact point is confirmed, so never stop on the carriageway. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit a tower and the sweep of cables into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for the deck and towers with less distortion. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the cable lines or the locks below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Shoot there only where it is legal and safe to stop, as no pull-off at that exact point is confirmed, and never stand on the carriageway. From the deck you can look back toward the Agua Clara side or the Fort San Lorenzo side. You get a close view of the cable-stayed deck and towers, with the locks visible below from either side of the span.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the cables up with the grid, so the towers look straight and not leaning. Keep the deck as a diagonal leading line into the frame. For a wider view of the whole bridge, the Agua Clara visitor centre shows the lock chambers in the foreground with the bridge far off.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower or sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the cables stay sharp. Hold the phone with both hands, since traffic on the bridge can make it shake.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the concrete and cables, and traffic may be lighter then.

text.access_note: This is a public road bridge with heavy traffic, so stop only where it is legal and safe; no pull-off at the stand-here point is confirmed. Check the official site before you go for the Agua Clara visitor centre.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the concrete and cables.

name: Agua Clara Locks
label: Agua Clara Locks
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.

notes: Visitor centre viewing platform over the expanded Panama Canal locks.

text.description:
Agua Clara Locks are a lock complex on the Colón map. The appeal is likely to be scale: large structures, long stretches of water and plenty of open sky give you strong lines to work with. A person in the foreground helps show how big everything is.

On a phone, work with the layers. Put something close to you at the bottom of the frame, such as a railing, a sign or a friend, then let the water, the structures and the sky fill the rest. Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, because straight edges make a tilted shot obvious. If something is moving through the scene, take a few frames a few seconds apart rather than one, and switch on Live Photos so you can choose the best moment afterwards.

The phone icon on the map is at the spot itself, so you are already in the right place. Take a wide shot first, then step closer and use the zoom for details. Weather can change quickly, so keep a dry cloth for your lens, as damp air and drizzle can smear it. Check for any access restrictions locally before you go.
text.geographic_location: Agua Clara Locks are on the Colón map.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Check a map app for the best route from where you are staying. The phone icon on the map is at the spot itself, so once you arrive you can use the map to find it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full width of the scene and the sky. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Put a railing, a sign or a person in the lower part of the frame, and let any straight edges run away from you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the horizon up with one of the horizontal lines. Let the straight edges in the scene lead the eye towards the water or the sky. Take one wide shot, then a closer one with the zoom. If something is moving, take several frames a few seconds apart.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright sky to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps its colour and the concrete does not wash out. Switch on Live Photos when something is moving so you can pick the best frame afterwards. Wipe the lens before shooting, as humidity can leave a haze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh reflections on the water than midday. Check access details locally before you go.

text.access_note: Check access details locally before you go.

name: Immaculate Conception Cathedral, Colón
label: Colón Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida Amador Guerrero & Calle 5ta' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Avenida Amador Guerrero and Calle 5ta (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q21515127: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: The Immaculate Conception Cathedral (Catedral de la Inmaculada Concepción) is the Catholic cathedral of Colón, a city in the north of Panama. It is the seat of the Diocese of Colón-Kuna Yala, which was created on 13 June 1997 and belongs to the ecclesiastical province of Panama. It photographs well because of its front. The main facade, with its twin bell towers and spires, is an upright, symmetrical subject that sits neatly in a phone frame. The street corner of Avenida Amador Guerrero and Calle 5ta gives the classic frontal view, so you do not need to hunt for an angle. Stand face the front of the building and let both towers fill the height of the screen. Switch on your phone's gridlines and line them up with the edges of the towers, so the building does not lean. Tap the facade to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright and the walls look washed out. Take one wide shot with the street in front for context, then a closer one of the towers using the telephoto lens. This is an active church, so be respectful if services are under way, and check current access before you go.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in the city of Colón, in the north of Panama.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stops serve this spot, so head to the corner of Avenida Amador Guerrero and Calle 5ta from the centre of Colón. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the facade. If the pavement is narrow and you cannot step back far enough, use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both towers in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spires.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Avenida Amador Guerrero and Calle 5ta (front (main facade) of the cathedral, facing the street corner). The frontal view of the cathedral's facade with its twin bell towers and spires.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre yourself on the doorway so the two towers look balanced, and use the gridlines to keep the vertical edges straight. Hold the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the towers lean inwards. Keep some street in the bottom of the frame to show the corner setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright. Take a few frames and keep the sharpest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the facade, and often fewer people on the street.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but the church may be closed or have restrictions inside, so check the official site or the diocese before you go and dress modestly if you enter.

label: Cristóbal Admin Bldg

notes: Historic Canal Zone-era port administration building at Cristóbal.

text.description:
The Cristóbal Administration Building (Edificio de Administración de Cristóbal) is a building on the Colón map, and it makes a straightforward subject for a phone photo. This page does not give its history, size or dates, so the advice here is about how to photograph it rather than its story.

The approach works best from a little way back. Start with the default lens (1x) and fit the full width of the building into the frame, with a bit of sky above and some ground below. If you cannot step back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the building near the middle of the frame so the edges do not stretch.

Once you have the full view, move closer and use 2x or more to pick out details such as the entrance, windows or signs. Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the edges of the building to keep the verticals straight. Tap the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright.

Check on arrival whether the area around the building is open to the public, and be considerate of others nearby.
text.directions_text: Once there, turn to face south. From there it is about 1 minute on foot to the building itself. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough. Use 2x or more for details such as the entrance or windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Face south and keep the building in the middle of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the edges of the building so the verticals stay straight. Leave a little sky above and ground below. Take one wide shot, then step in for a closer detail shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and take a few shots in case of blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light in the morning or late afternoon usually flatters a building like this. Avoid the middle of the day if the sun is high and bright.

text.access_note: Access and any restrictions around the building are not stated here, so check locally before you go.
